criteria.text: Given a customer selects a flight, hotel, and safari, when they proceed to checkout, then the system confirms the booking as one trip.
Given a customer selects unavailable dates, when they try to book, then the system shows an error message.
Trust: The system logs the booking transaction in the CRM.

stories.notes: Built in August (CC-20260828-b4k2, commit 423ed0b) and never ticked; checked against the code on 2026-10-05 (CC-20261005-7kcq), no code change needed. AC1: flight+hotel+safari confirm as ONE trip (one tripId, legs {flightId,hotelId,safariId}, status confirmed). AC2: an unavailable selection returns status unavailable with the message "One or more selections are not available." and creates no trip (it is also routed to an advisor, STORY-003). AC3: every confirmed booking is written once to the CRM transaction log (crmTransactionLog.js, idempotent by tripId, durable when COLABERRY_DATA_DIR is set). Failure paths also covered: declined payment, invalid customer, missing/malformed idempotency key, key reuse with different arguments. Known limits: inventory is an in-memory stand-in and the confirmed-bookings Map is per-process (the CRM log row is the durable trace).

Given a customer selects an unsupported destination, when they try to view details, then the system shows a message to contact an advisor.
Trust: The system logs customer interactions with the African section.

tests_added: backend/src/services/africa/safariDetailsService.test.js (9 assertions: happy path, unsupported destination, logging idempotency, missing safari details, system timeout capped at 2 attempts, timeout-then-retry recovery, throwing source not retried, invalid interaction key refused before any read, logInteraction rejects a bad key)

backend/src/services/africa/africanSectionService.test.js (10 assertions: browse the section, incomplete destination flagged not hidden, list flag agrees with the detail view, returned rows are copies, logging idempotency, empty-catalog boundary, system timeout, throwing source not retried, non-array source rejected as a contract violation, invalid interaction key refused)
stories.notes: All three criteria pass against executed tests, not inspection. Both suites exit 0. Failure paths from the story brief are all covered: unsupported destination, missing safari details, and system timeout (the last one was deferred by the original commit 9a52f6b and is closed here by putting the catalog behind an async source read through an explicit timeout with capped retries). Honest limits: there is no HTTP entry point yet, so the services are called directly rather than over a route, which means the auth and role-based-permission guardrail is not exercised here; and the catalog and interaction log are in-memory, so the audit trail does not survive a process restart. Both are inherited from the STORY-001 walking skeleton, not introduced by this story.

criteria.text: Given a customer makes an unclear request, when the system processes it, then it flags the request for advisor review.
Given a customer provides complete information, when the system processes it, then it does not flag the request.
Trust: The system logs all flagged requests for audit.

tests_added: backend/src/services/advisor/requestTriageService.test.js (11 groups: complete request not flagged, unclear request flagged, flag written to the audit queue, all 8 clarity rules firing individually, party-size boundaries 1 and 12 accepted, replay does not double-queue, 8 unusable inputs refused and never reported clear, audit rows are copies, queue rejects an unusable requestId, a rule that throws flags instead of passing, a failed audit write reported as flag_not_recorded with no advisor paged)

backend/src/services/advisor/advisorNotifier.test.js (7 groups: flagging notifies an advisor, replay does not page twice, notification timeout does not lose the flag, a throwing notifier is not retried and the flag survives, a failed notification can be retried later and succeed, a clear request pages nobody, an unusable review is refused)

backend/src/services/advisor/advisorRouting.test.js (8 groups, proving the wiring in BOTH directions: an unsupported destination and an unfinished catalog record reach an advisor with full context, an unavailable booking leg reaches an advisor, a retried booking does not duplicate the task, and a successful lookup, a declined payment and a non-routable outcome all create nothing)

backend/src/services/shared/jsonFileStore.test.js (7 groups, the important ones using TWO separate node processes against one data directory: an advisor review survives a real restart including its in-place notification update, idempotency holds across a restart, the CRM and interaction logs survive too, corrupt and wrong-shaped files refuse to load, the atomic write leaves no temp file)

backend/src/http/server.test.js (9 groups: a missing or malformed token table refuses to start, no credential / wrong scheme / bad token all return an opaque 401, a customer is refused the advisor queue while an advisor is allowed, a customer cannot submit as another customer, triage over HTTP flags and the advisor sees it, malformed / wrong-shaped / oversized bodies are refused at the boundary, 404 and 405 routing, African-section outcomes map to honest status codes, correlation ids echoed when valid and replaced when not)
stories.notes: All three criteria pass against executed tests. Triage is DETERMINISTIC by design - no model is consulted, because CLAUDE.md's core principle is that probabilistic components do not decide production outcomes and a safety requirement is the last place to put a coin flip. Governing bias is when-in-doubt-flag: unusable input returns invalid_request (deliberately NOT clear), and a clarity rule that throws counts as fired rather than passed, so a broken rule can never be the reason an unclear request slips through. All three named failure paths are covered: unclear-request-not-flagged (fail-safe defaults plus a test that makes a rule throw), flagged-request-not-logged (a failed audit write returns flag_not_recorded, pages nobody, and puts the reasons in the error log so the decision still leaves a trace), and advisor-notification-failure (the review row is written BEFORE any notification is attempted, so a failed page marks the row and never loses the flag; a failed page is not recorded as delivered, so a later retry can still reach the advisor). FOLLOW-UP WORK, done in the same session after the three criteria passed, closing the gaps this entry originally declared: (1) triage now validates the destination against the real catalog, so a well-formed request naming somewhere we do not sell is flagged instead of reading as clear - the 'plausible but wrong' hole is closed, and an unreadable catalog also flags rather than passing; (2) the advisor queue is now fed by the real customer journeys through advisorRouting.js - an unsupported destination, an unfinished catalog record and an unavailable booking leg all reach an advisor, while declined payments, invalid customer details and infrastructure failures deliberately do NOT, because a queue full of tasks no human can action is a queue advisors stop reading; (3) all three audit stores are durable via shared/jsonFileStore.js (atomic temp-then-rename write, opt-in through COLABERRY_DATA_DIR, corrupt file is fatal rather than silently empty), proven across real process restarts; and (4) there is now an HTTP boundary (backend/src/http, node:http only, no dependency added) with bearer-token authentication, role-based permissions, ownership checks, and input validation that rejects malformed bodies before they reach business logic. Remaining honest limits: nothing sends a real message - the default notifier writes to an in-memory outbox, since a real channel needs credentials this repo does not hold and CLAUDE.md forbids test sends; the file store rewrites the whole file per write and has no locking, so it is a bridge to Postgres and not a replacement; the auth layer is a token table from the environment, NOT the real authentication REQ-008 / STORY-006 owns, and that story's criteria are deliberately left unticked; and the triage rules still judge whether a request is well-formed and sold-by-us, not whether it is wise.

criteria.text: Given a completed transaction, when it is processed, then it should be logged in the accounting software.
Given a failed transaction, when it is attempted, then it should not be logged in the accounting software.
Trust: Given any transaction, when it is processed, then an audit log entry must be created.

stories.notes: Two stores, deliberately: the audit log records every transaction (criterion 3), the accounting client receives only completed ones (criteria 1 and 2). The audit entry is written BEFORE the accounting call and does not depend on it, so a transaction stays on record when the API is down. NOTHING MAKES A REAL HTTP CALL - the default transport is an in-memory ledger behind an injected post argument, same pattern as advisorNotifier.js, because no accounting vendor or credential exists for this repo. Booking now carries a price (AVAILABILITY Sets became Maps with priceCents; FL-100 + HT-200 + SF-300 = 4490.00 USD), agreed with the user rather than inventing a placeholder amount. Known limits: single currency, no refund/reversal path, single-process dedup (needs a Postgres unique constraint), and mcp/booking-desk/booking.py has not been ported and is now behind on pricing.

criteria.text: Given a customer logs in, when they enter correct credentials, then they access their portal.
Given a customer enters incorrect credentials, when they try to log in, then the system denies access.
Trust: The system logs all login attempts for security audit.

stories.notes: Login is scrypt (node crypto, no new dependency) with a per-user salt; the plaintext is never stored and the credential module has no logging surface at all. Sessions store only the token's SHA-256 digest, so the session file is not a list of working credentials - proven by a child-process test that reads the real portal-sessions.json off disk. Two clocks: 30-minute sliding idle timeout and a 12-hour absolute lifetime that never slides, so a stolen token cannot be kept alive by the thief's own activity. EVERY login attempt is audited - success, wrong password, unknown account, malformed submission, and blocked-by-lockout - keyed on a server-generated UUID, never the client's correlation id: the audit log is first-write-wins, so a replayed X-Correlation-ID would otherwise silence every attempt after the first (tested). An unauditable login is REFUSED and its session revoked, so no access is granted that cannot be accounted for. All four rejection reasons are byte-identical to the customer while the trail keeps the specific reason. Unknown users pay the full scrypt cost against a decoy hash, so response timing is not a user-enumeration oracle (108ms vs 110ms measured). 5 failures in 15 minutes locks for 15 minutes, checked BEFORE the password so a locked account buys no scrypt work. DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED BY ITS OWN TEST: the first draft derived the comparison key at the stored hash's length rather than the canonical 32 bytes, so truncating a stored hash produced one that still verified while comparing fewer bytes; an unexpected key length is now a flat refusal. SCOPE: REQ-007's 'view and manage' is satisfied on the VIEW half only - read-only itineraries, agreed with the user rather than half-building a mutation path. Cancellation needs refunds and an accounting reversal; change requests are STORY-003's advisor routing. A stranger's trip returns 404, not 403, byte-identical to a nonexistent trip, so trip ids cannot be walked to map the business. server.js crossed CLAUDE.md's 500-line hard ceiling, so per the Modular Composition Rule it was split before the new routes were allowed to stand: endpoints moved to backend/src/http/routes/ (portal, triage, advisor, africa), server.js kept the HTTP mechanics and dropped 561->348 lines. The split is a pure move, proven by re-running STORY-003's suite UNMODIFIED. NOT DONE, deliberately: role-based permissions beyond the two existing roles (STORY-006), advisor-on-behalf-of access, MFA, password reset/rotation, per-IP throttling (nginx's job at the edge), refresh tokens, and cross-process session locking (single-process store, same as every other store in this repo). Known trade-off: someone who knows a customer id can lock that account for 15 minutes.

criteria.text: Given a user logs in, when they have admin rights, then they access admin features.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/admin.test.js - an admin token reaches GET /api/admin/roles, POST /api/admin/roles and GET /api/admin/audit (each a distinct permission).

criteria.text: Given a user logs in, when they have customer rights, then they access customer features only.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/admin.test.js - customer and advisor tokens get 403 on every admin path while keeping their own routes; admin is 403 on portal trips and the advisor queue (admin is not a superuser).

criteria.text: Trust: The system logs all access attempts and changes in permissions.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/admin.test.js - the role change, the denied access attempt and the refused assignment are all readable through GET /api/admin/audit with actor, resource, required permission and correlation id.

stories.notes: RBAC is a permission table, not a role check. Routes used to declare `roles: [...]` in six separate files; they now declare one `permission`, and can(role, permission) in services/authz/permissions.js is the only way an access decision is made - hasRole() was DELETED rather than deprecated, because two mechanisms means the first route that picks the wrong one is a hole nobody sees. The swap is proven behaviour-preserving by STORY-003 and STORY-005's suites passing UNMODIFIED. Roles are NOT nested and admin is NOT a superuser: each role's grants are written out longhand, and admin deliberately lacks portal.trips.read and advisor.reviews.read, with tests asserting those absences so a later 'simplification' into a hierarchy fails loudly. Two sources of role: the directory (COLABERRY_API_TOKENS, which is how the bootstrap admin exists at all) and the assignment store, which overrides it. Roles resolve PER REQUEST, not at login, so a demotion bites on the next call rather than whenever a 12-hour session expires - tested end-to-end: a live session token gains the advisor queue and loses portal trips with no new login. Four assignment guards: not_permitted, self_assignment (nobody re-grades themselves, so an admin role change needs a second admin), last_admin (zero admins is a lockout nothing inside the system can undo), and unknown_role (the 'admn' typo, which reads like a grant and behaves like a lockout). Every refusal is audited, not just returned, through one refuse() helper so a sixth branch cannot forget. Assignment is write-ahead audited (pending -> success) so a crash mid-change cannot claim success. Routes are validated against the permission table at module load, so a route that forgets its permission or names one that does not exist stops the process instead of silently serving everybody or nobody - and that guard has its own test, without which it could be deleted and every other test would still pass. DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY ON AC-3: 403s get a durable audit row, 401s do not. A 401 is anonymous (no actor to attribute) and the audit store rewrites its whole file per row, so auditing them would hand any unauthenticated caller a disk-fill with quadratic write amplification; 401s are still fully recorded in the structured log stream. HONEST LIMIT: assignRole's not_permitted and last_admin refusals are UNREACHABLE over HTTP - the route's own permission check fires first for the former, and self_assignment fires first for the latter. Both are kept because assignRole is callable from a script with no boundary in front, and roleAssignments.test.js covers that path. NOT DONE, deliberately: per-resource scoping ('advisor for THESE customers'), time-bounded grants, approval workflows, bulk assignment, and audit-trail filtering by actor or date (needs query-string parsing, which the pipeline does not do yet). Advisor-on-behalf-of customer access remains unbuilt and is a separate permission when it is wanted, not a side effect of seniority. HARDENING PASS (same session): assignRole is synchronous end to end, so Node cannot interleave two calls and its read-then-write is atomic - but that guarantee was accidental and undefended, and one `await` inside it would silently reintroduce the race. It is now documented as load-bearing and defended two ways: a structural assertion that assignRole is not an AsyncFunction, and a real HTTP race. THE RACE CORRECTED AN EARLIER CLAIM: two admins demoting each other simultaneously DOES reach last_admin over HTTP, so this story's earlier note that it was unreachable held only for sequential requests and has been fixed in admin.test.js - the kind of note that invites someone to delete a guard as dead code. The loser's status is nondeterministic by design (403 if the second request had not yet been authenticated and per-request resolution had already stripped its admin role, 409 if it had); the test asserts the invariant - countAdmins never reaches zero - rather than pinning a code, which would be asserting the socket scheduler. Ten simultaneous identical promotions change the state once, audit the change once, and audit all nine no-ops. DURABILITY is now proven in child processes against a real COLABERRY_DATA_DIR, with the demotion direction tested separately because a lost promotion is a nuisance while a lost demotion is a silent re-grant; the last-admin guard is proven to count PERSISTED state, not the directory, or a fresh process would see two admins and demote the remaining one to zero. The documented recovery path is proven rather than asserted - a lost store falls back to directory roles, at the honest cost of undoing every demotion, with the audit trail (a separate file, proven untouched) being what tells you which changes to re-apply. STILL UNHANDLED, pre-existing and repo-wide: two Node processes sharing a data directory each hold their own in-memory Map and lose each other's writes. Documented in jsonFileStore.js; the real fix is Postgres, not something to bolt on inside this story.

criteria.text: Given a quote is generated, when a customer views it, then it displays without internal costs.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/quotes.test.js: the customer response is read as raw text and asserted to contain no cost total (854000), margin (166000) or unit cost (420000), no internal note, and no key matching /cost|margin|internal|supplier/i at any depth. quoteView.test.js repeats the scan after adding an unanticipated internal field. The same suite re-runs the scan on the REHYDRATED record, proving the allow-list filters a reparsed JSON object and not just the frozen one priceQuote returned.

criteria.text: Given a quote is modified, when it is saved, then the system updates the customer view.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/quotes.test.js: an advisor PATCHes to one line plus a 10% discount, then the customer's next GET /api/portal/quotes/:id returns version 2 at totalCents 900000 with the new note - read back through the API after the save, not from the write's return value. quotes.durability.test.js proves the revision survives a real restart in a separate process - a lost revision is silent, leaving a normal-looking quote at the old price.

criteria.text: Trust: The system logs all quote generations and modifications.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/http/quotes.test.js: quote.generated and quote.modified are both read back through GET /api/admin/audit with actor, resource, distinct correlation ids, and totalCentsBefore/totalCentsAfter on the modification.

stories.notes: Pricing is over explicit line items, not a backend rate card: mcp/trip-quotes already holds one and a JS copy would be a second source of truth for money. Customer and staff reads are separate endpoints with separate permissions and separate allow-list projections, so the customer route cannot reach the costed document at all. A quote that cannot be audited is rolled back rather than kept. Verified by npm run verify: 29/29 tests, mypy clean. Hardened after the first pass: every other suite runs in-memory, so a durability suite was added against a real COLABERRY_DATA_DIR in child processes - the quote, the revision, the audit trail, idempotency and the audit-failure rollback all verified across a restart. CI green on a clean machine. Known remaining: concurrency is atomic by construction (no await inside the write paths) but not yet asserted structurally.

criteria.text: Given a group booking is initiated, when details are complete, then the system confirms the booking for all members.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/booking/groupBookingService.test.js: a three-member group returns status confirmed with one entry per traveller, each carrying its own tripId and status confirmed, asserted with .every() rather than on a sample. The itinerary is asserted to be ONE object on the group and each member is asserted NOT to carry a copy of it, so all-or-nothing confirmation is structural rather than a loop that can succeed four times and fail the fifth. groupBooking.durability.test.js re-reads the group in a separate process against a real COLABERRY_DATA_DIR and asserts all three members and the shared itinerary survive intact: a booking that comes back with two of its three travellers is the same partial confirmation arriving by another route.

criteria.text: Given a group booking is incomplete, when submitted, then the system prompts for missing information.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/booking/groupValidation.test.js: 21 checks asserting the CONTENT of the prompt, not merely that it refused - a validator that rejects everything with an empty list would pass "it refused" and still fail this criterion. Covers a missing organizer, itinerary and members list; each itinerary leg named individually; non-object itineraries and members; group size below 2 and above 25 including the boundary itself; blank member ids and names; duplicates, including the regression where a duplicate went unreported behind an otherwise-broken member; and "too long" reported distinctly from "required". A rejected value is asserted never to appear in the prompt. groupBookingService.test.js re-checks it end to end: an incomplete submission returns at least 3 problems in one pass, charges nobody, stores no row, and leaves getCustomerRecord at not_found.

criteria.text: Trust: The system logs all group booking transactions.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/booking/groupBookingService.test.js: group_booking.confirmed is read back from the audit trail with actor, resource, memberIds and totalCents, and asserted NOT to contain any traveller name. One booking-log row per member is asserted at their own SHARE rather than the group total - mutation-tested, since swapping perPersonCents for totalCents fails the suite with "a member's lifetime value is their own share", which is what stops a three-person safari reading as three safaris sold in crm/customerRecord.js. Exactly one accounting entry carries the group total against the organizer. Refusals are audited too (group_booking.refused with a reason and a problem count, and no submitted values), and a declined card is audited while asserted absent from the ledger. groupBooking.durability.test.js proves the audit entry and every member row survive a restart, and that an unauditable group is rolled back from the JSON file itself - mutation-tested against a jsonFileStore whose delete does not reach disk.

stories.notes: Service-layer only, no HTTP route - the booking domain is fronted over MCP, as STORY-005 is. AC-1: one group record holds the shared itinerary and all members, so all-or-nothing confirmation is structural rather than a loop that can partially succeed. AC-2: groupValidation.js returns every problem at once, naming positions and never echoing submitted values. AC-3: audit entry per confirmation AND per refusal, one booking-log row per member at their own share, one accounting entry for the group total against the organizer. 43 checks across three suites; durability proven in separate processes against a real data dir.

criteria.text: Given a customer provides preferences, when AI processes them, then it suggests relevant trips.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/suggestions/suggestionEngine.test.js and backend/src/http/suggestions.test.js. Over HTTP, POST /api/suggestions/trips with {countries:["Tanzania"], interests:["wildlife"]} returns exactly SF-300 at score 1 with its reasons spelled out ("in Tanzania, which you asked for", "matches your interest in wildlife"), asserted as an EXACT list rather than a non-empty one - a test for "some suggestions came back" would pass against a service handing everyone the whole catalog. Relevance is enforced two ways and both are tested: a relevance floor of 0.5 over the dimensions the customer actually stated, and a hard exclusion for a trip matching NONE of the stated interests. That second rule was added because the suite caught the hole: before it, a customer asking for a BEACH trip in Botswana was answered with a Botswana SAFARI, which took the country credit and cleared the floor on country alone. Budget and duration exclude rather than deduct past a named stretch band (15%, 2 days), so a trip at triple the budget is absent, not merely last, and a near-miss shows at half credit and says out loud that it is over. Scoring is pure and deterministic: the same request twice is asserted to produce the identical object.

criteria.text: Given a customer provides no preferences, when AI processes, then it suggests popular trips.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/suggestions/suggestionEngine.test.js, tripCorpus.test.js and backend/src/http/suggestions.test.js. A request with no preferences returns strategy "popular" straight off the corpus order, reasoned as "one of our most-booked trips", and all four spellings of saying nothing - undefined, null, {}, and {countries:null} - are asserted to take the same path. The ordering is total and stable (editorial country rank, then tripId), so the test asserts an exact ordered list instead of a set. The case this would otherwise pass vacuously is covered in tripCorpus.test.js: the authored product book is EMPTY on a cold start, so the corpus falls back to the seeded catalog - without that fallback this criterion would have been green against an empty list. A half-filled seeded record (SF-301, name and country only) is skipped rather than suggested with no price. Honest caveat: popularity is an EDITORIAL country ordering written into tripCorpus.js, not a measurement - this repo has no view counts or ratings and the booking ledger is empty on a cold start. It is one function (rankFor) to replace when a real signal exists.

criteria.text: Trust: The system logs all AI suggestions for review.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/suggestions/tripSuggestionService.test.js and backend/src/http/suggestions.test.js. Every terminal outcome writes an audit row - suggestions.generated on success, suggestions.failed on an engine error, suggestions.refused on malformed input - and the success row is read back through GET /api/admin/audit as an admin, not merely from the module store. The row is asserted on CONTENT, not existence: strategy, confidence, the tripIds and their scores, which preference dimensions were stated, the engine attempt count and the flag reasons. A row saying only "suggestions happened" cannot answer the question the log exists to answer. The actor is the AUTHENTICATED principal (asserted as CUST-SUGG-1), never anything the body claimed. Rows are keyed on requestId via deriveAuditKey, so the same request twice leaves ONE row and the response reports replayed:true - asserted by counting rows through the admin API. The load-bearing choice: if the audit write fails the service REFUSES to serve (suggestions_not_auditable, 503) rather than handing over suggestions it cannot account for, tested with a throwing audit. Preference VALUES are deliberately absent from the row - only the dimension names - and that absence is asserted.

stories.notes: THE GOVERNING DECISION, agreed with the user before any code was written: the "AI module" is a deterministic scorer behind a swappable port, not a model call. CLAUDE.md core principle is that probabilistic components do not decide production outcomes, REQ-011 asks for suggestions and not for a technology, and a live model would have meant a paid external dependency, a secret, and acceptance tests that cannot be deterministic. The engine is one function of one argument - suggestTrips({preferences, trips, limit}) - matching the shape shared/callWithRetry.js wraps, so a model-backed engine drops in at a single call site and inherits the timeout, capped retries, audit trail and advisor flag without any of them changing. The service is already tested against engines that throw, hang and return the wrong shape, so the envelope is proven before anything remote arrives. API surface only, no UI - same as STORY-007, 008, 013 and 015 in this repo, which has no frontend. The customer surface is one endpoint, POST /api/suggestions/trips. GUARDRAILS. Uncertain requests reach a human on exactly three conditions: zero suggestions despite stated preferences, a matched result at or below 0.6 confidence, and an engine error. A popular-strategy result is deliberately NOT flagged - somebody who stated nothing has not made an uncertain request, and flagging every browse would bury the queue the guardrail depends on. The review row is keyed sugg:<requestId>, not the bare requestId, because advisorReviewQueue is first-write-wins and requestTriageService already writes to it; sharing the key would mean a request that was triaged AND asked for suggestions could hold only one of the two flags, with the other vanishing silently. No advisor is paged: the queue row is the source of truth, and paging a human when a browse returns a thin match is how an on-call rota stops being answered. AUTHZ. One new permission, suggestions.request, granted to customer and advisor only. Deliberately NOT bundled with catalog.read, which it most resembles: browsing is a read, asking for suggestions WRITES an audit row every time and may write to the advisor queue. sales, product_manager and admin are each asserted to get a 403. KNOWN GAPS, deliberately not built. Popularity is editorial, not measured (see criterion 2 evidence). Suggestions are not persisted - only the audit row is, so there is no "show me my last suggestions" read route; the trail is admin.audit.read. No free-text wishes: preferences are a structured object and unstructured requests remain advisor/requestTriageService.js job. No dates or seasonality (no date model exists in this repo), no party size (it changes the price, not which trips suit, and quotes/ owns price), no personalisation from history, and no caching. Interest tagging is literal substring matching against a small explicit vocabulary - it will miss tags, which costs a trip one point, rather than over-tag, which would make every trip match every preference and is the irrelevant-suggestions failure path arriving through the back door. VERIFICATION: npm test 47/47 passing, npm run typecheck clean.

criteria.text: Given a supplier is added, when details are saved, then it appears in the supplier list.
Given a supplier is updated, when changes are saved, then the system reflects the updates.
Trust: The system logs all supplier data changes.

stories.notes: Supplier book with contracts and rates (REQ-012), advisor-only. Four data-mismatch faults refused: inverted/zero-length contract dates, duplicate contractRef, orphan rate, rate currency disagreeing with its contract. Updates validate the MERGED record, not the patch - replacing a contract is legal in isolation but orphans the rates already stored against the old ref. Every create, update, no-op save and refusal is audited; a mutation with no correlationId is refused rather than performed unaudited. supplierStore.js is over the 500-line ceiling with the deviation logged in its header per CLAUDE.md.

criteria.text: Given a payment is made, when processed, then the system updates the balance.
Given a payment fails, when retried, then the system processes it again or shows an error.
Trust: The system logs all payment transactions.

stories.notes: Balance is per payment account (one per customer per trip, opened by the new finance role), because bookTripService charges the full price at booking and so never leaves a balance; the booking path is untouched. The balance is DERIVED from total minus succeeded payments on every read, never stored, so it cannot go stale. Payments reuse the STORY-001 mock processor and the STORY-004 transactionRecorder: every attempt is audited before anything else, only successes post to accounting. Retries are keyed on paymentId: a succeeded payment never charges again, and a charge whose balance write failed is found in the audit log on retry and finished without a second charge. The charge itself has a 10s timeout and is never auto-retried (a timeout does not prove nothing was charged). AC2 "processes it again" is proven with an injected processor in customerPaymentService.test.js; over HTTP the mock always declines CUST-DECLINED, so the HTTP test proves the "shows an error" half. Follow-up: permissions.js is 554 lines, over the 500-line ceiling (was 526 before this story); splitting the role table out is logged separately.

criteria.text: Given data is available, when analytics are generated, then they display revenue and booking trends.
Given data is incomplete, when analytics are generated, then the system highlights missing data.
Trust: The system logs all analytics generation activities.

stories.notes: GET /api/analytics/revenue (new analytics.read permission, granted to a new manager role and to finance - NOT admin, which reads the audit trail of analytics runs) returns monthly revenue and booking trends computed from the CRM booking log on every call. Incomplete rows are excluded and named per field (status partial); duplicate tripIds and mixed currencies are flagged as mismatch (revenue withheld, never summed across currencies); an empty log is no_data, not $0. Every generation, including a failed one, is audited keyed on the request correlation id; if the audit write fails no figures are returned (503 audit_unavailable). An unreadable log is 503 source_unavailable. permissions.js was split (vocabulary moved verbatim to permissionCatalog.js) to get it back under the 500-line ceiling before adding the grant. Revenue is booked revenue: refunds and cancellations are not subtracted.

criteria.text: Given a new trip request, when a travel advisor creates a proposal, then it should be completed within 30 minutes.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/proposals/proposalClock.test.js, proposalStore.test.js and backend/src/http/proposals.test.js. The clock is SERVER-stamped at startProposal before any work happens and no later write touches it - proposalStore.test.js asserts startedAt is unchanged after completion, which is the assertion that makes this criterion mean anything: a completion that re-stamped the start would issue every proposal in zero minutes and pass vacuously forever. Confirmed by mutation: re-stamping startedAt at completion fails proposals.durability.test.js. A draft opened 09:00 and issued 09:12 reports within_sla with elapsedMs 720000, asserted by hand rather than recomputed. The 30-minute boundary is tested to the millisecond on both sides (29:59.999 and 30:00.000 pass, 30:00.001 breaches) because within 30 minutes includes the mark. Over HTTP, POST /api/proposals returns deadlineAt and remainingMs so the advisor can see the target, and proposals.durability.test.js measures a 41-minute elapsed across a real process restart.

criteria.text: Given a trip proposal, when it exceeds 30 minutes, then the advisor should be notified of the delay.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/proposals/proposalDelayNotifier.test.js, proposalStore.test.js and backend/src/http/proposals.test.js. A late proposal STILL ISSUES and is marked breached - refusing at 30:00 would destroy the advisor's work to satisfy a timer - and the page is part of completeProposal rather than something a route remembers to ask for: proposalStore.test.js asserts a 41-minute completion pages once and an on-time one pages nobody. The other half of the criterion is covered too: listBreachedOpenProposals finds a draft that is ALREADY late but not yet issued, since a proposal abandoned at minute 12 and resumed at minute 90 would otherwise never page anyone. Over HTTP, a seeded 100-minute-old draft appears in GET /api/proposals/sla/breaches and POST /api/proposals/sla/notify pages its advisor with overdueMinutes at least 70. Dedup is keyed on the DURABLE audit log rather than an in-memory Set, so proposals.durability.test.js proves a restart does not re-page an advisor already told, and the same proposal completing later reports already_notified instead of paging twice. Caveat recorded honestly: the default channel is an in-memory outbox, as advisor/advisorNotifier.js is - no real message is sent, and a test asserts that default so a real channel cannot be wired in silently.

criteria.text: Trust: Given any trip proposal, when it is created, then an audit log entry must be created.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/proposals/proposals.audit.test.js, proposals.durability.test.js and backend/src/http/proposals.test.js. Both writes go through the shared audited-commit door (backend/src/services/shared/auditedCommit.js), which reads the write back and ROLLS IT BACK if the audit throws - so an unaudited proposal cannot exist rather than merely being unlikely: with a failing audit, store size is asserted to be 0 on open, and on completion the row is asserted to roll back to the open draft with its clock intact. proposal.opened and proposal.issued are keyed on the version (proposalId:proposal.opened.v1, proposalId:proposal.issued.v2) so the audit log's first-write-wins rule cannot swallow the second, and both are read back through GET /api/admin/audit rather than only from the module's own store. Refusals are audited too, and the trail is asserted to carry ids and figures only - no customerNote or internalNotes text reaches it. proposals.durability.test.js confirms both entries and the recorded elapsed time survive a real restart.

stories.notes: API surface only, no UI. The story's how-to-build-it says develop a user interface; this repo has no frontend and STORY-007/008 both shipped services plus HTTP routes only, so the advisor surface is five endpoints under /api/proposals. Deviation agreed with the user before any code was written; all three criteria are fully testable at the service and route layer. THE LOAD-BEARING DECISION: startedAt is written durably before any work and never rewritten. AC-1 is measurable, AC-2 works for an open draft and not only a finished one, and a crash cannot hide an overrun - all three fall out of that one choice. Got wrong, the system would not break, it would flatter itself: every restart would silently reset every clock and no proposal would ever be late. The 30-minute boundary is INCLUSIVE (a breach is strictly greater than 30:00.000), tested to the millisecond on both sides. A backwards clock (skew, DST) clamps to zero and reads as on time with clockWentBackwards set, because paging an advisor about a minus-four-minute delay teaches them to ignore the channel. An unreadable clock is recorded as a breach with slaUnknown and null figures - of the two ways to be wrong, on time is the one that suppresses a page the advisor is owed. The elapsed time is STORED at issue, not derived on read. Recomputed from startedAt it would grow forever, and an on-time proposal would look breached by the next morning. Notification dedup is keyed on the durable audit log, not an in-memory Set, so a restart cannot re-page. The entry is written AFTER a confirmed send, which leaves a one-page duplicate window on a crash between send and audit; write-ahead would close that window but a failed send would then suppress the page forever with the trail claiming otherwise. A duplicate page is a nuisance, a suppressed page is the missed alert the criterion exists for. The routes take no at and no startedAt - the clock is the server's, always, because an SLA the measured party can edit is not an SLA. A test posts a forged future at to the sweep and asserts it pages nobody. To test a 30-minute breach in a suite that runs in milliseconds, proposals.test.js SEEDS a genuinely 100-minute-old draft through the service with a controlled clock and then exercises the real endpoints; nothing in the production path was loosened. quoteWriteGuard.js (STORY-007) was refactored into a thin adapter over the new shared door. Behaviour-preserving and verified as such: the audit key, both refusal messages, the log service tag, all three log event names, the quoteId log field and the rollback were each checked byte-for-byte, because a shared helper that quietly renames an audit key is a break in the trail, not a tidy-up. Known gaps, deliberately not built: nothing in production passes the assemble hook yet (pricing is local and synchronous, so nothing in completion CAN hang) - the boundary exists so STORY-015's itinerary read inherits the timeout and capped retries instead of inventing its own, and it is tested with hanging, throwing and junk-returning stubs. No customer-facing proposal view (the customer's priced document is a quote, and STORY-007 owns it). No conversion of an issued proposal into a quote - doing both atomically needs a transaction across two stores. Any advisor may read or complete a colleague's proposal; the story says nothing about ownership and desk work gets covered, so there is a named test recording that as a decision rather than an oversight.

criteria.text: Given a new lead, when it is added to the CRM, then it should be visible in the lead list.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/crm/leadStore.test.js and backend/src/http/crm.test.js - POST /api/crm/leads returns 201 and the lead is then present in GET /api/crm/leads, with createdBy taken from the resolved principal rather than the request body.

criteria.text: Given a customer booking, when it is completed, then it should update the customer's booking history.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/crm/customerRecord.test.js and backend/src/http/crm.test.js - a booking driven through the real bookTrip() appears in GET /api/crm/customers/:id with its tripId, amount and legs, and the customer moves from 404 to 200; a replayed booking does not double-count the lifetime value, and a payment_failed booking never becomes history.

criteria.text: Trust: Given any CRM entry, when it is modified, then an audit log entry must be created.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/crm/leadStore.test.js and backend/src/http/crm.test.js - crm.lead.created, crm.lead.updated (with before/after per field), crm.lead.unchanged and crm.lead.refused are all readable afterwards through GET /api/admin/audit with actor, resource and correlation id; a SECOND edit to the same lead is asserted to produce its own distinct entry.

stories.notes: The CRM is two halves with different owners of truth. LEADS are new state (services/crm/leadStore.js). CUSTOMERS and BOOKING HISTORY are NOT: booking/crmTransactionLog.js is already written by bookTripService at the moment a booking confirms, so services/crm/customerRecord.js is a read model over it and acceptance criterion 2 needed no new state at all - the history updates because the history IS the booking log, with no sync step to fall behind. A CRM bookings table would have been a second answer to 'what has this customer bought?', and the second answer is the one that goes stale the first time a booking is amended. The same reasoning is already written out at portal/itineraryService.js:11. A FOURTH ROLE, not a widened advisor. The story's persona is a sales manager and no such role existed. permissions.js' own header predicted this ('when a fourth role arrives ... only this table does'), and the alternative - giving advisor the CRM grants - would have required DELETING the line directly above it that says advisor gets 'NOT customer data by default'. A rule you delete to make today's story fit is not a rule. ADMIN DELIBERATELY DOES NOT GET THE CRM either: an admin can grant the sales role and that act is audited, but cannot quietly read the lead book, which keeps 'admin is not a superuser' true. crm.leads.read and crm.leads.write are split (a read exposes the whole book at once, a write corrupts one record at a time), and crm.customers.read is split from both because a booking history is more sensitive than an enquiry. permissions.test.js asserts sales holds exactly those three and that customer, advisor and admin each hold none, so a later 'simplification' into a role hierarchy fails loudly. THE SUBTLE BUG THIS STORY HAD TO AVOID. Audit entries are first-write-wins, a trap auditLog.js:213 documents explicitly. A module that keyed every edit on '<leadId>:updated' would have recorded the FIRST edit to a lead and silently discarded every later one - an audit trail that looks complete and is not, which is worse than no trail at all. Lead EDITS therefore key on the caller's per-request correlationId, while CREATES key on the freshly generated leadId (collision-free by construction). There is a regression test that makes two successive edits and asserts both entries exist and differ. The consequence is stated as a rule rather than left implicit: a mutation arriving with no correlationId is REFUSED rather than performed unaudited, because the project guardrail is that all changes are audited, so 'I cannot audit this' has to mean 'I will not do this'. Lead duplication is deduped on normalised (email + source), the key CLAUDE.md mandates for lead capture. A repeat POST returns the ORIGINAL row with replayed: true and HTTP 200 rather than 201, so a client retrying a submission it is unsure about can tell whether it captured the lead or found it already there; the first row wins, so a duplicate cannot re-attribute the lead to whoever submitted it second. The same email from a DIFFERENT source is intentionally a separate lead - a partner referral is a different commercial event from the same person filling in the web form, and sales needs both rows. The same rule is enforced on the edit path (duplicate_lead, 409), because an edit that moves a lead onto another lead's email+source is the same duplicate arriving through the other door. Validation is split on a line borrowed from adminRoutes.js:98. The ROUTE checks only the envelope ('is this a JSON object?'); the SERVICE judges the fields. Rejecting a malformed email at the boundary would have returned the same 400 to the caller while quietly losing the audit entry - a refused lead that leaves no trace. So a non-object body is invalid_request_body and never reached a decision, while a bad email is invalid_lead, audited, and reported with EVERY problem at once rather than one per round trip. Refusals are audited too, and the audit entry does not echo the rejected value back, since it arrived from outside and ends up in log lines. Unauthorized data access is not handled in the CRM code at all, on purpose: routes DECLARE a permission and http/server.js enforces it once and audits every refusal, so a second check inside the CRM would be a second policy that can disagree with the first. crm.test.js therefore tests it at the boundary, across all five routes x three wrong roles (customer, advisor, admin) for 403, plus anonymous for 401 - because each route names its own permission and passing one proves nothing about the other four. It also proves the indirection pays for itself: granting sales to a live customer token opens the CRM and revoking it closes it again, with no restart. Records handed to callers are frozen, leads and customer records alike, so the only way to change a lead is updateLead, which is the only thing that writes an audit entry. createdAt and createdBy are outside the editable allow-list - an 'update' that can rewrite who captured a lead and when is not an update, it is a way to erase the trail. Fields outside the allow-list are REFUSED by name rather than silently dropped, because silently dropping them tells the caller the save succeeded; the legal half of a mixed patch does not apply either. A malformed percent-sequence in a path id is a 400 rather than an unguarded decodeURIComponent throw, which would have been a 500 on a URL a scanner finds within the hour. NOT DONE, deliberately. No cross-customer revenue aggregate: lifetimeValueCents is a per-account relationship figure, and revenue and booking analytics is STORY-012's job - two modules computing the business's revenue ends as two different numbers on two dashboards. No customer directory: identity already belongs to portal/portalCredentials.js and a CRM copy would be both a second truth and a second place to leak a contact list from, so 'customer' here means 'someone with a confirmed booking' and a person with none is a LEAD - a coherent split rather than a gap. No lead deletion ('lost' is a status, and erasing a lead erases the audit trail's subject), no lead-to-customer conversion flow, no lead owner assignment, no merge of two leads found to be the same person, and no pagination on either list - both reads are O(n) scans, and STORY-016 is the scalability story, so an index (which is a second copy of the data that can desync) waits for a measured reason. HONEST LIMITS. Reads are not audited, only modifications and denials - the criterion is about modification, and auditing successful reads means an entry per page view, which buries the entries that record a change; if it is wanted later it belongs at the boundary, once, not scattered through read models. Mixed currencies on one account are collected into a currencies array rather than assumed, so a total summed across unlike currencies is visible as such instead of being quietly wrong, but nothing yet CONVERTS them. Persistence is still jsonFileStore (in-memory unless COLABERRY_DATA_DIR is set), so the pre-existing repo-wide limit applies unchanged: two Node processes sharing a data directory each hold their own in-memory Map and lose each other's writes. The real fix is Postgres, not something to bolt on inside this story.

criteria.text: Given a new safari product, when it is created, then it should include itineraries and pricing.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/products/safariProductValidation.test.js, safariProductStore.test.js and backend/src/http/products.test.js. A product is not storable without BOTH halves: the itinerary must be a non-empty array whose days are exactly 1..durationDays, and the pricing block must carry a currency, a per-person price above zero and a cost. POST /api/products/safari returns 201 with the itinerary in full - days asserted as [1,2,3], the day-2 title and location checked by value - and the pricing with its margin DERIVED rather than supplied: 520000 - 420000 = 100000, written out by hand rather than recomputed from the implementation's own formula. createdBy comes from the resolved principal, never from the request body, so a caller cannot nominate who authored a package. The created product is then read back through GET /api/products/safari/:id and asserted deepStrictEqual to what the POST returned, and through the list, where count is 1. A second identical POST is 200 with replayed: true rather than 201, creates no second row and writes no second audit entry.

criteria.text: Given an existing safari product, when its itinerary is updated, then the changes should be reflected immediately.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/products/safariProductStore.test.js and backend/src/http/products.test.js. A PATCH replacing day 2 is visible on the VERY NEXT request through both doors into the book - the single GET and the list - with version at 2, updatedBy set to the editing principal, createdBy unchanged, and the two days that were not edited asserted still exactly as they were. The response reports changed: ["itinerary"] rather than claiming a blanket save. The other half of immediacy is asserted too, and is the part that would otherwise rot: a REFUSED edit leaves the stored product byte-identical, checked with deepStrictEqual against the pre-edit record after a below-cost reprice, after a duration change that orphans day 3, after a duration change that leaves days 4-5 unsold, and after every 403 from an advisor, customer, sales and admin token. A store that refuses an edit and half-applies it is worse than one that accepts a bad edit, because the product manager is told no and the catalog says otherwise. Re-sending the same itinerary in a different order, or a name with different whitespace, is correctly reported as no change and does not bump the version.

criteria.text: Trust: Given any safari product, when it is created or updated, then an audit log entry must be created.
criteria.evidence: backend/src/services/products/safariProductStore.test.js and backend/src/http/products.test.js - products.safari.created, products.safari.updated, products.safari.unchanged and products.safari.refused are all readable AFTERWARDS through GET /api/admin/audit with actor, resource and correlation id, which is a stronger proof than reading the module's own store. Updates key their audit entry on the CALLER'S correlationId, not on the product id, and a SECOND edit is asserted to write its own distinct entry: keyed on the product id, auditLog.js's first-write-wins rule would have recorded the first change to a package and silently discarded every later one, so a package repriced three times would show its original price in the trail forever. The consequence is stated and tested: a mutation arriving with no correlationId is REFUSED rather than performed unaudited, and the product is asserted unchanged after it. The update entry names fields: ["itinerary"] and daysChanged: [2] - which day moved, not merely that something did - and the itinerary is recorded as the digest {days: 3} deliberately, because auditLog.js's context depth cap would have turned a full before/after pair of day objects into "<truncated>", producing an entry that looked complete and held no evidence.

stories.notes: 43/43 npm test (was 40/40), npm run typecheck clean, so npm run verify green end to end. THE ITINERARY-CONFLICT RULE IS ONE SENTENCE, NOT THREE CHECKS: the set of days must be exactly 1..durationDays, each appearing once. That catches all three real faults - two entries claiming one day, a day past the duration, and a gap that is unsold time mid-package - each reported as its own named problem. Out-of-order input is VALID and gets sorted, because refusing a reordered form submission is rigour that only hurts the user. THE UPDATE PATH VALIDATES THE MERGED RECORD, NOT THE PATCH, and that is where this story actually bites: {durationDays: 2} on a 3-day product is a perfectly legal patch in isolation that would leave the stored itinerary describing a day which no longer exists, and replacing the itinerary alone can leave a gap against the stored duration. Both have named regression cases. costPerPersonCents is REQUIRED because without it there is no margin and the below-cost refusal - the check that catches $5,200 typed as 5200 cents - can never fire; cost and margin are nested under pricing.internal so a future customer-facing projection has exactly one field to filter, which is also why products.read is staff-only today. PRICING IS REPLACED AS A BLOCK, not merged field by field, so a patch omitting singleSupplementCents drops it to 0 - asserted explicitly so it is a decision rather than a discovery. A NEW product_manager ROLE rather than a wider advisor, chosen by the operator against the cheaper alternative: giving the product grants to advisor was one fewer row in the permission table in exchange for every advisor being able to reprice any package the agency sells. An advisor holds products.read - sell from the book, do not author it - and the HTTP suite asserts exactly that: 200 on both reads, 403 on POST and PATCH. The one change outside this story was approved first and TIGHTENS a test: permissions.test.js's CRM block warned that a loop over ROLES would silently pass the day a fifth role arrived with CRM access, so product_manager is now asserted by hand to hold none. Deliberately not built: no seasonal or per-date pricing (the backend holds no rate card - STORY-007's reasoning, and a quote carries the season), no per-traveller tiers, no link from a product to the africa/catalogSource.js destination it visits, no DELETE route (erasing a product erases the subject of its own audit trail), no pagination - list and the duplicate check both scan, O(n) on purpose, because STORY-016 owns scale and an index is a second copy of the data that can desync. NO DURABILITY SUITE YET: the store uses the same jsonFileStore as every other store here and inherits its behaviour, but unlike STORY-007/008/013 that has not been proven for THIS module in separate processes, and it is the most valuable thing to add next. version is recorded but NOT enforced - two product managers editing at once is last-write-wins, the standing repo-wide limit, and the real fix is Postgres.

criteria.text: Given an increase in user load, when multiple advisors access the system, then it should maintain performance.
Given a surge in customer activity, when thousands of customers interact with the system, then it should not crash.
Trust: Given any system load, when it scales, then performance metrics must be logged.

stories.notes: Bounded concurrency with a bounded wait queue, rolling latency percentiles, a public health probe the load balancer reads as 200-healthy / 503-drain-me, and a perf_snapshot JSON line on an interval. 117/117 npm test (was 80/80). AC-1: 40 advisors x 5 simultaneous requests, all 200, zero shed, zero failed, p95 inside a stated 500ms budget. AC-2: 2,000 requests from 1,000 distinct customers, every accepted connection answered with a 200 or a clean 503, zero dropped, probe back to healthy and traffic served afterwards with no intervention. AC-3: a real perf_snapshot line captured off the log stream carrying p50/p95/p99 and describing that load, plus /api/admin/metrics gated to ops.metrics.read (advisor and customer both 403) and a public probe asserted to leak no capacity figures. Failure paths: overload (slots held, every request cleanly refused with Retry-After, recovery without intervention), network latency (an abandoned request releases its slot - a leak would permanently cost capacity) and database bottleneck (store write amplification MEASURED at N/2, ceiling documented at 10,000 rows / ~2.1MB per synchronous write, asserted in bytes not milliseconds so it is reproducible). server.js was split to wire.js first, as a pure move, to respect CLAUDE.md's 500-line ceiling before adding code. KNOWN LIMIT, documented in docs/SCALABILITY.md: peak_in_flight is 1 because handlers are synchronous once admitted, so the event loop is the real serialiser - the bound governs AWAITING work and bites once a handler waits on a database or supplier API. Postgres not attempted: database-engine change is a governance boundary.
